excerpt: When the at-fault driver's policy is not enough: UM/UIM coverage, additional defendants, and the other routes to full compensation.
keyTakeaways: When policy limits are insufficient, recovery options include your own UM/UIM coverage (in South Carolina UM is mandatory under S.C. Code § 38-77-150 and UIM must be offered under § 38-77-160; in Georgia UM/UIM is included unless rejected in writing under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11), claims against multiple parties, umbrella policies, employer liability, personal assets, and the failure-to-settle claim against the at-fault driver's insurer. Georgia's statutory bad-faith penalties (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6; § 33-7-11(j) for UM claims) run only against your own insurer.

faqs.question: What are the minimum insurance limits in GA and SC?
faqs.answer: Both states require 25/50/25: $25,000 per person bodily injury, $50,000 per accident, $25,000 property damage. Often insufficient for serious injuries.

faqs.question: What is UIM coverage and how does it help?
faqs.answer: UIM pays when your damages exceed the at-fault driver's limits, up to your UIM limits. South Carolina requires uninsured-motorist coverage on every policy (S.C. Code § 38-77-150) and requires insurers to offer UIM up to your liability limits, which you may accept or decline (§ 38-77-160). Georgia includes UM/UIM in every policy unless you reject it in writing (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11); whether it pays on top of the other driver's limits or only the difference depends on the 'added-on' or 'reduced-by' election on your policy.

faqs.question: Can I sue the at-fault driver personally?
faqs.answer: Yes. If they have personal assets — real estate, savings, investments — you can pursue a judgment. Collecting can be difficult if assets are limited. Your attorney can conduct asset searches.

faqs.question: Can I file claims against multiple parties?
faqs.answer: Yes. If multiple parties contributed to your accident, you can file separate claims against each. Common in multi-vehicle, trucking, and product liability cases.

faqs.question: What is a bad faith claim?
faqs.answer: If your own insurer — for example your UM/UIM carrier — unreasonably refuses to pay a valid claim, you may have a bad faith claim: in Georgia a statutory penalty of up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6; up to 25% or $25,000 on UM claims under § 33-7-11(j)); in South Carolina attorney's fees after a 90-day demand (S.C. Code § 38-59-40) and a common-law bad-faith claim for actual, consequential and punitive damages (Nichols). Neither state lets you sue the other driver's insurer for bad faith; when that insurer wrongly refuses to settle within its limits, the claim for the excess belongs to the at-fault driver (Holt in Georgia; Tyger River in South Carolina) and is usually assigned to the injured person.

faqs.question: How does a lawyer help recover more than policy limits?
faqs.answer: An attorney identifies all recovery sources: UM/UIM, multiple parties, umbrella policies, employer liability, and bad faith claims. They conduct investigations, asset searches, and policy reviews to maximize every dollar available.
